(i) the evolution of senescent mortality and fecundity is affected by kin competition, (ii) the evolution of age-specific fecundity is influenced by dispersal and (iii) dispersal and kinship can produce antagonistic pleiotropic patterns affecting vital rates at various ages.

(i) kin competition reduces the strength and changes the sign of selection on age-dependent vital rates; (ii) limited dispersal increases the strength of selection for a broad distribution of fecundity over the lifetime, which slows down reproductive senescenc; (iii) limited dispersal and the presence of kin competition may favour ‘suicide genes’, i.e. mutations increasing mortality without other direct pleitropic effects, but only when age-specific fecundity decreases rapidly.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of kin competition and natal dispersal in shaping senescence and the age structure of populations.
the evolution of life history and ageing.
the evolutionary forces that shape the life-history of a species.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evolutionary theory of senescence is still in its infancy.

the evolution of ageing is not a trivial consequence of the trade-off between reproduction and survival, as is often suggested, and the evolution of senility may be a complex process involving a variety of factors.
dispersal and kin selection can slow down ageing, but only if the rate of senescence is not too rapid.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the evolutionary dynamics of senescence are more complicated than previously thought.
limited dispersal can slow down the evolution of senescent decline of fecundity, while kin competition accelerates the evolution of senile death.
limited dispersal and the social structure it generates may be an important determinant of the evolution of senescent patterns in nature.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the evolution of senescent traits in natural populations is not necessarily the outcome of a simple trade-off between current and future reproduction, but can also be influenced by the social context in which individuals live.
the evolution of senescent traits in nature may be more complex than the classical models of antagonistic pleitropy and disposable soma would predict.
the evolutionary forces acting on age-specific vital rates are not necessarily the same as the forces driving senescence.
